tagline: Old highway segments connect mountain hairpins, roadside inventions and a bent river crossing.
intro: Historic Route 66 links surviving highway segments, with interstates connecting the designated pieces in Arizona. Near Oatman, Sitgreaves Pass brings hairpin curves and steep grades; New Mexico offers prairie, rocky outcrops and adobe villages. FHWA lists Historic Route 66 as both an All-American Road and a National Scenic Byway, emphasizing its history and roadside atmosphere.

The numbered highway began in 1926, assembled from existing roads rather than built anew. Cyrus Avery helped campaign for the Chicago–Los Angeles route, and the highway association formed in 1927 to promote paving, maintenance and tourism. Interstates later diverted its traffic, and the U.S. highway designation ended in 1985. In Seligman, barber Angel Delgadillo organized local business owners in 1987 to form the Historic Route 66 Association of Arizona. Their lobbying brought state historic-route designations that November, giving sections of the bypassed highway a new identity as a destination.

Traveling east from Oatman, the Arizona historic road runs toward Kingman and Seligman, with another section from Flagstaff to Winona. In New Mexico, portions pass motels and diners with restored neon signs. Oklahoma brings Oklahoma City and Tulsa; farther east, the Mississippi crossing leads into Illinois, through Springfield and Pontiac toward Chicago. New Mexico Tourism advises carrying maps to negotiate old alignments among modern highways.

moments.title: Oatman
moments.text: Oatman’s fortunes followed gold first and highway traffic later. The opening of the Tom Reed mine and a 1915 discovery at United Eastern brought a gold rush to the Black Mountains. United Eastern stopped operating in 1924. The remaining gold mines were ordered shut by the federal government for the war effort, which needed other metals. The town then served Route 66 travelers between Kingman and Needles, until a new alignment bypassed it. By the 1960s it was almost abandoned. Its present Route 66 identity includes wooden sidewalks and wild burros wandering the streets.

moments.title: Blue Whale of Catoosa
moments.text: The Blue Whale began as an anniversary gift, before it became a Route 66 attraction. Hugh Davis and Harold Thomas built it from iron and concrete, and Davis revealed it to his wife Zelta on their 34th wedding anniversary in 1972. She collected whale figurines. The pond was intended for family use, but Davis added sand, picnic tables and lifeguards as local swimmers began arriving. After closure and disrepair, a community restoration effort returned the whale to its original blue in 1997. The City of Catoosa bought the property from the Davis family in 2020.

moments.title: Chain of Rocks Bridge
moments.text: A 22-degree bend interrupts the Chain of Rocks Bridge halfway across the Mississippi. During construction, a water intake and bedrock unable to support parts of the bridge required that change of direction. Privately built as a toll bridge in 1929, it later carried Bypass U.S. 66 past downtown St. Louis. A new bridge opened to the north for I-270 in 1966, and the old crossing closed in 1970. Local trails group Trailnet leased the crossing in 1998, before Great Rivers Greenway took over the lease in 2014. Renovation gave the old bridge a different purpose: its crossing now carries walking and cycling trails.
moments.notice: Notice the bend in the middle of the river crossing.
